snip.t: Autoimmune diseases (e.g., SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) treated with immunosuppressants.

Medication history: *Current antibiotics, antiretrovirals, antimalarials, immunosuppressants, recent drug allergies?* — Prior antibiotics select resistant flora; drug interactions affect choice of agents.
Intrinsic Renal: Treat the specific cause (e.g., antibiotics for pyelonephritis, immunosuppressants for glomerulonephritis, stopping nephrotoxic drugs).
Medication / allergies: Recent antibiotics, immunosuppressants, drug allergies — Influences choice of empiric agents and need for desensitisation
Medication & allergies: Current drugs (especially immunosuppressants, antiretrovirals), drug allergies — Guides choice of empiric agents and avoids adverse reactions.
Medications: *Recent antibiotics, immunosuppressants, antihistamines?* — Certain drugs (e.g., ceftriaxone) can cause immune complex reactions; antihistamines may mask early signs.

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP): IVIG or PE (induction) → oral steroids or steroid‑sparing immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate) — Physiotherapy, occupational therapy

qs.q: In a patient receiving steroids and immunosuppressants, which intra‑operative factor most directly compromises wound healing?
o: Selection of suture size and gauge.
qs.e: Gentle tissue handling preserves blood supply, crucial when healing is already impaired. Suture size influences strength but not the primary healing cascade.

ai.title: Immunosuppressants in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Immunosuppressants modulate the immune system to treat autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, but increase infection risk. In low‑resource settings, drug choice, monitoring and infection prevention are critical.

sections.p: Immunosuppressants are drugs that reduce immune activity, used for autoimmune diseases, organ transplantation and severe inflammatory conditions. Diagnosis is clinical: identify the underlying immune‑mediated disease and assess need for immunosuppression.
b: Identify disease (e.g., SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis, transplant rejection).
Confirm active inflammation with history, exam and basic labs (ESR, CRP, CBC).

sections.p: Severity is gauged by disease activity scores (e.g., SLEDAI for lupus, DAS28 for RA) and organ involvement. Staging guides intensity of immunosuppression.
b: Mild: limited joint or skin disease, low activity scores.
Moderate: organ involvement, moderate scores, systemic symptoms.
Severe/life‑threatening: renal, CNS, pulmonary or vascular involvement.

sections.p: The need for immunosuppression arises from autoimmune disorders, transplant rejection, and some severe infections that trigger hyper‑inflammation.
b: Autoimmune: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease.
Transplant: kidney, liver, heart, bone‑marrow.
Severe post‑infectious inflammation (e.g., TB meningitis adjunct steroids).
Tropical considerations: SLE overlapping with malaria, HIV‑related immune reconstitution.

sections.p: Patients needing immunosuppression present with organ‑specific symptoms (joint swelling, rash, proteinuria) and systemic signs (fever, weight loss). In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation is common.
b: Joint pain with swelling and morning stiffness (RA).
Malar rash, photosensitivity, renal proteinuria (SLE).
Abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea (ulcerative colitis).
Graft dysfunction signs after transplant.

sections.p: When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues (e.g., persistent fever, weight loss for TB) and treat empirically if risk is high.

t.b: Detect cytopenias from disease or drug toxicity; low neutrophils raise infection risk.
Assess inflammatory activity; high values support need for stronger immunosuppression.
Confirm autoimmune diagnosis; guide drug choice (e.g., cyclophosphamide for severe lupus nephritis).
Baseline for drug safety; monitor for toxicity.
Detect proteinuria or hematuria indicating renal involvement.
Screen for pulmonary infection before starting high‑dose agents.

t.a: TB screening (Mantoux or GeneXpert if possible)
t.b: Identify latent TB; treat before initiating biologics or high‑dose steroids.

sections.p: Immunosuppression predisposes to opportunistic infections, malignancy and drug‑specific toxicities.
b: Fever, cough, weight loss → suspect TB, fungal infection.
New skin lesions or lymphadenopathy → consider lymphoma.
Persistent cytopenias → bone‑marrow suppression.

sections.p: Start with the least toxic agent that controls disease, add steroids for rapid control, and monitor for infection.
b: Corticosteroids: rapid anti‑inflammatory effect; taper as soon as possible.
Antimetabolites (azathioprine, mycophenolate): steroid‑sparing, oral, inexpensive.
Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus): useful in transplant and severe vasculitis; monitor renal function.
Alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide): for life‑threatening organ disease; avoid in pregnancy.
Biologics (TNF‑α inhibitors, rituximab): reserved for refractory cases; costly, infection risk high.
Avoid long‑term high‑dose steroids in diabetics, hypertensives, or active infections.

sections.p: Regular clinical review, lab monitoring and infection prophylaxis are essential.
b: CBC, LFT, renal panel every 2–4 weeks for the first 3 months, then every 3 months.
Vaccinate before starting therapy (influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B).
Provide TMP‑SMX prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii if CD4 < 200 or on high‑dose steroids.
Educate patients on early infection signs and when to seek care.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic immunosuppression or require similar drugs.
b: Infection‑induced cytopenias (e.g., malaria) vs drug‑induced marrow suppression.
Steroid‑induced hyperglycaemia vs new‑onset diabetes.

sections.p: Laboratory values may be altered by the disease itself or by the drugs.
b: CRP may be normal in patients on high‑dose steroids despite active disease.
Liver enzymes can rise from azathioprine toxicity or from viral hepatitis common in the region.

faq.q: Why are steroids used first even though they have many side effects?
faq.a: They act quickly to control inflammation, buying time to start slower‑acting agents while limiting organ damage.

faq.q: Can I give a biologic in a patient with latent TB?
faq.a: Treat latent TB first; starting a biologic without treatment risks reactivation.

faq.q: What monitoring is essential for azathioprine?
faq.a: Baseline and periodic CBC and liver tests; watch for leukopenia or transaminase rise.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with SLE presents with new proteinuria – what is the next step and why? — Check renal function and start induction therapy (cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate) to prevent irreversible kidney damage.
A transplant patient on tacrolimus develops a fever and cough; what should you consider? — Evaluate for opportunistic infection (TB, Pneumocystis) before adjusting immunosuppression.
Why is TMP‑SMX prophylaxis recommended for patients on high‑dose steroids? — It prevents Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, a life‑threatening infection in immunosuppressed hosts.
How would you differentiate steroid‑induced hyperglycaemia from new diabetes in a patient on prednisone? — Check fasting glucose before steroids, assess timing of rise, and consider HbA1c trends.
A patient on azathioprine develops leukopenia; what is your management? — Stop azathioprine, monitor counts, consider dose reduction or switch to mycophenolate.
What are the contraindications for using cyclophosphamide in severe lupus nephritis? — Pregnancy, active infection, severe bone‑marrow suppression, and uncontrolled hypertension.
Explain why biologic therapy is avoided in a patient with active hepatitis B. — Reactivation risk is high; antiviral prophylaxis is required or alternative therapy chosen.
In a low‑resource setting without GeneXpert, how would you screen for latent TB before starting a TNF inhibitor? — Use Mantoux test or chest X‑ray; if high risk, treat empirically for latent TB.
